Build a factor with explicit, verified levels

Source: R/categorical_guard.R
grdlvls.Rd

Creates a factor whose levels you write out in full and in order, instead of letting factor() sort them alphabetically. The first level is the reference category of every regression fitted on the factor, so writing the levels out decides the baseline on purpose. Values outside the declared levels are an error, and you can assert which level is the reference so that a later edit to lvls cannot change it unnoticed.

Usage

grdlvls(x, lvls, ref = NULL)

Arguments

x

Character or factor vector. A factor is read through its labels.

lvls

Character vector of every allowed level, in the intended order. The first element is the reference category.

ref

Optional character string, default NULL (no check). When given it must equal levels[1]; use it to state the intended baseline next to the code that fits the model.

Value

A factor with exactly the levels in levels, in that order.

Details

The function checks that every non-missing value of x is in lvls, then returns factor(x, levels = levels). Declared levels that do not occur are kept as empty levels (they still appear in tables with a count of zero).

Errors:

  • lvls not a non-empty character vector, or containing NA;

  • a value of x not in lvls (listed in the message);

  • ref given and not identical to levels[1].

See also

grdrcd, audcats.

Examples

# reference category chosen on purpose, not by alphabet
g <- grdlvls(c("White", "Black", "White"), c("White", "Black"), "White")
levels(g)
#> [1] "White" "Black"

# a declared level that does not occur is kept, with a zero count
table(grdlvls(c("a", "a"), c("a", "b")))
#> 
#> a b 
#> 2 0 

# a stray value, or a reference that is not first, is refused
try(grdlvls(c("White", "Blak"), c("White", "Black")))
#> Error : grdlvls: values outside the declared levels: ‘Blak’
try(grdlvls(c("White", "Black"), c("White", "Black"), ref = "Black"))
#> Error : grdlvls: declared reference ‘Black’ is not levels[1] (‘White’); reorder `lvls` so the reference is explicit and first.
